kpis.name: Total unique orders
kpis.limitations: The export is a snapshot cut on 2018-10-17. Orders created after that date do not exist, and a small number of very recent orders are still in non-terminal states (shipped/processing).
kpis.notes: One order_id = one order; an order can contain several item lines.

kpis.name: Total merchandise sales
kpis.filters: every fact_order_item row; ALL order_status values included
kpis.limitations: Freight is excluded (it is reported separately). Non-delivered orders (canceled/unavailable) are still included as gross merchandise value, so this is list-price sales, not recognised revenue. Prices are BRL and not inflation-adjusted.
kpis.notes: Order-level merchandise sales always come from this sum; the ETL column fact_order_summary.item_revenue is GROSS (price + freight) and is never used as sales.

kpis.name: Total freight charges
kpis.eligible_population: same 112,650 item units as merchandise sales
kpis.limitations: Freight is what the customer was charged, not the carrier's true cost. It is reported per item line, so it cannot be split by seller without aggregating item lines.

kpis.name: Average order value (AOV)
kpis.formula: merchandise sales / orders that contain at least one item
kpis.filters: merchandise sales exclude freight; denominator excludes orders with no line items
kpis.limitations: Orders with no line items (no product record) cannot have a basket value and are excluded. Using all orders as the denominator gives R$ 136.68, which understates a real basket because empty orders are treated as R$ 0. Freight is not part of AOV.
kpis.notes: Alternative denominator: all 99,441 orders -> R$ 136.68. Including freight per order would raise the figure by about R$ 22.82.

kpis.name: Delivered orders
kpis.limitations: 'delivered' is the status at export time. A handful of delivered orders lack a customer-delivery timestamp in the source, so the delivered count is 2 higher than the orders with a usable delivery date.
kpis.notes: 2 delivered orders have no customer-delivery date and are excluded from duration/lateness KPIs.

kpis.name: Delivery completion rate
kpis.limitations: This is a status share, not a true cohort conversion: orders created just before the export cut are still in transit and depress the rate slightly. It also counts orders that were delivered late.

kpis.name: Cancellation rate
kpis.limitations: Only orders that reached the marketplace are visible; requests cancelled before an order_id was created are not in the data. 'unavailable' orders (failed fulfilment) are a separate status and are not counted as cancellations.

kpis.name: Average review score
kpis.filters: every review row; the ETL keeps one review per order (latest answer)
kpis.limitations: Reviews are voluntary and left soon after delivery, so they over-represent early experience and under-represent silent dissatisfaction. Scores of 1-2 are conventionally treated as negative.

kpis.name: On-time delivery rate
kpis.formula: orders delivered on/before estimate / orders with a delivery date
kpis.filters: order_delivered_customer_date IS NOT NULL; is_late_vs_estimate = 0 (delivered at or before the estimated date)
kpis.limitations: Denominator excludes orders with no delivery timestamp (2,965), which includes some never-delivered orders; excluding them flatters the rate. The estimate itself is a commercial promise that can be padded, so a high rate is not the same as a fast delivery.

kpis.name: Late delivery rate
kpis.formula: orders delivered after estimate / orders with a delivery date
kpis.limitations: Complement of the on-time rate; it is 'late vs the promise', not an absolute service level. Orders with no delivery record are neither on time nor late and are excluded from both.
kpis.notes: 2,965 orders (2.98%) have no delivery timestamp and sit outside this KPI.

kpis.name: Average delivery duration
kpis.formula: AVG(days from purchase to customer delivery)
kpis.limitations: Calendar days, not business days. The mean is pulled up by a long tail (up to 210 days); the median/percentiles are more robust and are shown in the findings report. Non-delivered orders are excluded.

kpis.name: Repeat customer rate
kpis.limitations: customer_id is regenerated per order, so customer_unique_id is required to link a person's orders. The export window is only ~2 years, so customers who would return after the cut are not observed and the rate is a lower bound. Guests are pooled only by the identity key the source provides.

kpis.name: Average items per order
kpis.formula: total item units / orders with >= 1 item
kpis.filters: sum of fact_order_summary.n_items over orders with items
kpis.limitations: 'Item' is an order line (order_item_id), not a distinct product: the same product twice in one order counts twice. Orders with no items are excluded.

kpis.name: Payment method distribution
kpis.formula: SUM(payment_value) by payment_type / total payment value
kpis.filters: every bridge_payment row (an order can carry several payment records)
kpis.limitations: Grain is the payment attempt, not the order: a voucher + card order appears twice, so shares by row do not sum to order shares. 'not_defined' and a few non-positive voucher rows exist and are retained, not silently dropped.
kpis.notes: Primary value is the credit-card share of payment value; full mix is in `detail`.

findings.title: Like-for-like growth: H1 2018 versus H1 2017
findings.business_question: Is the marketplace growing once the incomplete start and end of the export are removed?
findings.method: Sum merchandise sales (SUM of item price, freight excluded) and order counts for the two fully-observed half-years Jan-Jun 2017 and Jan-Jun 2018, then compute the year-over-year percentage change.
findings.result: H1 2017 = R$ 2,040,997.16 across 14,611 orders; H1 2018 = R$ 5,635,712.25 across 41,187 orders. YoY merchandise-sales growth = 176.1%; YoY order growth = 181.9%.
findings.period_population: Jan-Jun 2017 and Jan-Jun 2018; all 99,441 orders in the export, item-bearing lines only for sales
findings.interpretation: The two half-years are calendar-matched and fully covered, so this is a fair like-for-like comparison. Sales grew 176.1% while orders grew 181.9%: order volume grew faster than sales, so the average basket compressed modestly. The two components point to different levers, so both are reported.
findings.recommendation: Treat H1 2018 as the run-rate for planning rather than the partial tail of 2018. Track the sales-per-order and orders-per-customer components separately to see which is driving growth.
findings.limitations: Two half-years are a short series and the platform's customer mix and pricing changed between them. No inflation adjustment is applied to BRL figures.
findings.correlation_note: Growth is a descriptive time comparison, not a causal model: no intervention is isolated here.
findings.headline: Merchandise sales rose 176.1% year over year in H1 (H1 2017 vs H1 2018), with orders up 181.9%.

findings.title: Strongest trading month and Q4-2017 acceleration
findings.business_question: When does demand peak, and how strong is the Q4 seasonal lift?
findings.method: Rank complete months by merchandise sales; compare Q4 2017 (Oct-Dec) with Q3 2017 (Jul-Sep). Only months inside the full-volume window are ranked.
findings.result: Peak month = 2017-11 with R$ 1,010,271.37 and 7,544 orders (lowest complete month: 2017-01). Q4 2017 sales = R$ 2,418,404.97 vs Q3 2017 = R$ 1,696,404.85, a quarter-on-quarter change of 42.6%.
findings.interpretation: The November spike is consistent with Black-Friday promotional demand; the Q4 lift being concentrated in a single month suggests event-driven rather than broad secular demand.
findings.recommendation: Plan logistics and inventory capacity around the Q4 event peak. Because the lift is event-driven, provision for the peak months rather than an even seasonal ramp.
findings.limitations: One observed Q4 (2017) cannot separate a recurring seasonal effect from a one-off campaign; November 2017 may also reflect platform maturity rather than a seasonal pattern.
findings.correlation_note: The association with Black Friday is plausible context, not a controlled measurement: the dataset does not include marketing spend or campaign flags.
findings.headline: November 2017 was the peak month at R$ 1,010,271.37; Q4 2017 was 42.6% above Q3 2017.

findings.title: Incomplete periods are excluded from trends but always reported
findings.business_question: Which parts of the timeline cannot support trend conclusions?
findings.method: Flag the first and last calendar months as partial, and treat months before the full-volume window (2017-01) and after it (2018-08) as ramp-up / truncated; count them explicitly.
findings.result: Data spans 2016-09-04 to 2018-10-17. 20 complete months are used; 5 months are excluded (2016-09, 2016-10, 2016-12, 2018-09, 2018-10) holding 349 orders and R$ 49,930.92 of sales. Calendar months with no orders at all: 2016-11.
findings.interpretation: The 2016 months are platform ramp-up with negligible volume, and September-October 2018 are cut off by the export date. Including them would distort trend lines and averages.
findings.recommendation: Report trend metrics on the complete window and label the ramp-up/tail months as such in the dashboard; never chart the partial tail as if it were a collapse in demand.
findings.limitations: The completeness window is a judgement anchored to observed volume, not an external calendar of the business; revisit it if a longer export becomes available.

findings.title: Sales are concentrated in a few categories
findings.business_question: Is category revenue diversified or dependent on a handful of categories?
findings.method: Rank categories by merchandise sales, compute the share of the top 5 and the leading category.
findings.result: 74 categories. Largest = 'health_beauty' with R$ 1,258,681.34 (9.26% of sales); smallest non-zero = 'security_and_services' with R$ 283.29 (0.002% of sales). Top 5 categories = 39.74% of all merchandise sales.
findings.period_population: one row per (category, order) pair - 99,470 pairs across all item-bearing orders
findings.interpretation: Revenue depends on a narrow set of categories, so supplier or logistics disruption in those categories has an outsized effect on the platform.
findings.recommendation: Protect continuity for the top categories (inventory, seller relationships) while treating long-tail categories as optional growth experiments rather than core revenue.
findings.limitations: Sales are list prices and include non-delivered orders; category names come from the product catalogue and a few products have no category mapping.
findings.correlation_note: Concentration is a structural fact, not a causal finding.
findings.headline: The top 5 of 74 categories generate 39.74% of merchandise sales; 'health_beauty' leads with 9.26%.

findings.title: Category satisfaction and punctuality vary widely
findings.business_question: Which product categories satisfy customers, and which run late?
findings.method: Restrict to categories with at least 100 orders; compare average review score and the category late-delivery rate (share of delivered orders past the estimated date, computed once per order).
findings.result: Best-reviewed: 'books_general_interest' 4.463/5; worst-reviewed: 'office_furniture' 3.618/5. Highest late rate: 'audio' 12.9%; lowest: 'air_conditioning' 4.1%. Spearman correlation between a category's sales and its review score = -0.022.
findings.interpretation: Some low-volume or logistically awkward categories consistently under-perform on satisfaction and punctuality, while high-volume categories are not automatically the worst-rated.
findings.recommendation: Investigate the worst-reviewed and latest categories for handling/packaging or seller concentration before spending on demand; review-score gains compound through repeat purchase and word of mouth.
findings.limitations: Category review averages can hide seller-level problems, and the 100-order threshold is a stability rule, not a significance test.
findings.correlation_note: The category sales-vs-score correlation (-0.022) is an association across categories; it does not show that selling more causes lower scores.

findings.title: Demand is concentrated in the South-East
findings.business_question: How geographically concentrated is the customer base?
findings.method: Count orders and distinct customers per customer_state; compute the top-state and top-3-state shares.
findings.result: Sao Paulo (SP) = 41.98% of orders and R$ 5,202,955.05 of sales. Top 3 states = 66.61% of orders (SP, RJ, MG).
findings.interpretation: The marketplace is South-East-centric, which shapes delivery economics: most orders ship within a dense region, so national averages under-represent the cost of long-distance delivery.
findings.recommendation: Prioritise fulfilment and carrier coverage in SP/RJ/MG where volume and basket justify investment; test long-haul lanes separately because their freight and lateness behaviour differs.
findings.limitations: State is taken from the customer address at order time; a handful of customers moved between states (their orders are attributed to the address on each order).
findings.correlation_note: Geography is an observed distribution, not a causal driver by itself.
findings.headline: Sao Paulo alone is 41.98% of orders and 66.61% comes from just three states (SP, RJ, MG).

findings.title: Average basket differs by state, but volume and basket are not aligned
findings.business_question: Do high-volume states also have high-value baskets?
findings.method: For each state compute average merchandise sales per item-bearing order (SUM of item price divided by distinct orders), then compare the most populous state with the highest-basket state.
findings.result: Largest state SP: average basket R$ 125.75 over 41,375 orders. Highest-basket state (with meaningful volume): PB at R$ 216.67.
findings.interpretation: Basket size and order volume are separate dimensions; high-volume states are not necessarily high-basket states, so a single national AOV hides real mix differences.
findings.recommendation: Segment retention and assortment decisions by state cluster rather than nationally; use basket size, not just volume, to decide where to invest in logistics.
findings.limitations: Freight is excluded from the basket, and small states can show volatile average baskets that should not be over-read.
findings.correlation_note: This is a descriptive comparison, not evidence that geography changes willingness to pay.

findings.title: Most customers buy only once
findings.business_question: What share of customers return for a second order?
findings.method: Group all orders by customer_unique_id, count customers with >= 2 orders, and divide by all distinct customers. customer_unique_id is used because customer_id is regenerated per order.
findings.result: 2,997 of 96,096 customers placed 2+ orders = a repeat rate of 3.12%. Repeat customers placed 6,342 of 99,441 orders and generated R$ 778,821.97 (5.73% of merchandise sales).
findings.period_population: 96,096 distinct customers over the full export window
findings.interpretation: The business is acquisition-led: the overwhelming majority of customers transact once. Repeat customers are few but, per customer, are much more valuable.
findings.recommendation: Test a post-delivery retention programme (service follow-up, next-purchase incentive) targeted at first-time buyers; even a small lift in the repeat rate has a leveraged effect on sales.
findings.limitations: A ~2-year export window truncates the tail: customers who would return after the cut are counted as one-time, so the true repeat rate is a lower bound. Guest checkout may also split a person across identities.
findings.correlation_note: Repeat status and value are jointly observed; the data cannot show that repeat buying causes higher spend per se.
findings.headline: Only 3.12% of customers placed a second order, yet they generated 5.73% of merchandise sales.

findings.title: Repeat customers spend more and rate similarly
findings.business_question: Are returning customers worth more or happier than one-time buyers?
findings.method: Compare average review score for one-time versus repeat customers, and report the median days between a repeat customer's first and last order.
findings.result: Average review score: one-time = 4.084, repeat = 4.110. Median first-to-last span among repeat customers = 33 days.
findings.interpretation: Repeat customers contribute disproportionate value through cumulative spend. Similar satisfaction scores suggest retention is driven by need and assortment rather than by a service gap between the groups.
findings.recommendation: Focus messaging on the second purchase while the median return window is still open; measure whether the return interval shortens after the campaign.
findings.limitations: Per-customer spend is cumulative across orders, so comparing totals against one-time buyers is expected to favour repeat customers. Scores are simple averages and not weighted by order value.
findings.correlation_note: Higher cumulative spend for repeat customers is mechanical (more orders); it is not evidence of a causal retention premium.

findings.title: Card dominates, boleto is a material minority, vouchers fund part-payments
findings.business_question: Which payment methods carry the transaction value?
findings.method: Aggregate bridge_payment by payment_type and compute each method's share of total payment value.
findings.result: Total payment value R$ 16,008,872.12 across 103,886 payment records. credit_card = 78.34% of value, boleto = 17.92%, voucher = 2.37%, debit = 1.36%.
findings.period_population: all payment records (an order may have more than one)
findings.interpretation: Card is the backbone of collections, but a meaningful slice pays by bank slip (boleto), which has different settlement timing and failure modes and should not be ignored in checkout analytics.
findings.recommendation: Keep boleto and voucher paths well-instrumented; monitor decline/conversion by method rather than reporting a single 'payment success' number.
findings.limitations: Grain is the payment attempt, not the order: voucher + card orders appear twice, so row counts and value shares are by payment, not by basket. A few 'not_defined' rows exist.
findings.correlation_note: Payment mix is a distribution, not a causal relationship.

findings.title: Installments are widely used and track order size
findings.business_question: How often do customers split payments, and does basket size drive it?
findings.method: Compute the share of payment records with more than one installment and compare average payment value for multi-installment versus single-payment records.
findings.result: 49.42% of payment records use more than one installment. Average value: multi-installment R$ 196.76 vs single R$ 112.42 (75% higher).
findings.period_population: all payment records with a known installment count
findings.interpretation: Installment plans are close to a default behaviour rather than an exception, and they are used more on larger tickets, which is what one would expect if affordability, not method choice, drives the split.
findings.recommendation: Keep installment options visible at checkout for mid/high-ticket baskets; monitor default/chargeback rates by installment band, since longer plans change credit risk.
findings.limitations: The dataset records installment count, not interest paid or default outcome, so the cost and risk of installment selling cannot be measured here.
findings.correlation_note: The positive association between basket value and installment count is consistent with affordability pressure, but it is a correlation: product mix and promotions also move both.

findings.title: Late delivery is strongly associated with low review scores
findings.business_question: How much lower are review scores when a delivery misses its estimated date?
findings.method: Join reviews to the late/on-time flag (delivered orders with an estimate), compare average score and the share of 1-2 star reviews, and compute point-biserial (Pearson) and Spearman correlations.
findings.result: On-time orders average 4.294/5 over 88,168 reviews; late orders average 2.565/5 over 7,662 reviews (difference 1.729 points). Negative (1-2 star) review share: on-time 9.2% vs late 54.1%. Pearson r = -0.365, Spearman rho = -0.294.
findings.period_population: 95,830 reviewed, delivered orders with a late/on-time flag
findings.interpretation: The gap is large and consistent: late deliveries are the single clearest correlate of poor satisfaction in this dataset. The effect is visible both in average score and in the concentration of 1-2 star reviews.
findings.recommendation: Prioritise lateness reduction as a satisfaction lever: proactive delay notifications and expedited recovery on at-risk orders are more likely to protect scores than generic service messaging.
findings.limitations: Reviews are voluntary, so only reviewed orders enter this KPI, and the late/on-time split excludes orders with no delivery timestamp. Review scores are ordinal and coarse (1-5).
findings.correlation_note: This is a strong association, not proof of causation. Lateness may co-occur with long-distance routes, problem sellers, or peak-season congestion that independently depress scores; a controlled comparison holding those factors constant is needed before claiming that lateness alone causes dissatisfaction.

findings.title: Month-level on-time rate moves with the month-level review score
findings.business_question: Does satisfaction track punctuality over time as well as across orders?
findings.method: Join the monthly on-time delivery rate to the monthly average review score over complete months and compute their Pearson correlation (an ecological correlation).
findings.result: Across 20 complete months, correlation between monthly on-time % and monthly average review score = 0.776. On-time ranged 78.6%-98.6%; review score ranged 3.75-4.28.
findings.interpretation: The order-level relationship also appears at the month level, which makes the pattern harder to dismiss as an artifact of a single bad week.
findings.recommendation: Use punctuality as a leading operational indicator for satisfaction in the dashboard and investigate months where on-time falls before review scores follow.
findings.limitations: An ecological correlation across months can differ from the individual-level relationship and is sensitive to a few months; it is supporting evidence, not a substitute for the order-level analysis.
findings.correlation_note: Ecological correlations do not establish individual-level causation and may be confounded by seasonality or platform growth.

findings.title: Seller revenue is highly concentrated
findings.business_question: How dependent is the marketplace on its largest sellers?
findings.method: Rank sellers by merchandise sales and compute the share held by the top 1%, 5% and 10% of sellers.
findings.result: 3,095 sellers. Top 1% of sellers = 26.07% of merchandise sales; top 5% = 53.30%; top 10% = 67.56%.
findings.interpretation: A minority of sellers supplies most of the value, so seller churn or quality problems at the top have platform-level consequences.
findings.recommendation: Run a key-account programme for the top decile (service levels, inventory visibility) and keep a bench of qualified backup sellers for the top categories.
findings.limitations: Seller sales are gross merchandise value before returns/cancellations and exclude freight; sellers with no items are not represented.
findings.correlation_note: Concentration is a structural measurement, not a causal relationship.
findings.headline: The top 1% of sellers generate 26.07% of sales and the top 10% generate 67.56%.

findings.title: Lateness is not uniform across sellers
findings.business_question: Is late delivery a platform-wide problem or a seller-specific one?
findings.method: For sellers with at least 30 evaluable orders, describe the distribution of the late-delivery rate and correlate it with average review score (Spearman).
findings.result: Among 634 sellers with >= 30 evaluable orders, mean late rate = 7.8%, 90th percentile = 14.6%. Highest-late seller: ede0c03645598cdfc63ca8237acbe73d (late 34.9%, review 3.52). Spearman correlation between seller late rate and review score = -0.451.
findings.interpretation: The spread is wide, which means a substantial part of the lateness problem is addressable at the seller level rather than being an unavoidable platform-wide condition.
findings.recommendation: Use a late-rate threshold to trigger seller coaching or reduced placement, and track the worst decile monthly; target the tail rather than the average.
findings.limitations: Small sellers have noisy rates, which is why a 30-order floor is applied; seller lateness also reflects carrier and route, which the data attributes to the seller.
findings.correlation_note: The negative late-rate/review association is cross-sectional and confounded by product, price and geography; it is a correlation that supports prioritisation, not a causal claim that lateness alone drives the score.
findings.headline: Among 634 sellers with >= 30 orders, the mean late rate is 7.8% but the 90th percentile reaches 14.6%.

findings.title: Freight rises with weight, but per-kg cost falls sharply
findings.business_question: How does freight scale with product weight, and where is the freight burden concentrated?
findings.method: Bucket item units by product weight and compute average freight and freight-per-kg per bucket; correlate unit weight with freight across all known-weight units (Pearson and Spearman).
findings.result: Freight is 16.57% of merchandise sales overall. Freight per kg falls from R$ 112.70 in the 1. 0-200 g bucket to R$ 4.03 in the 6. 5001+ g bucket, while absolute average freight rises from R$ 14.74 to R$ 39.81. Weight-vs-freight correlation: Pearson 0.610, Spearman 0.447.
findings.period_population: 112,624 item units with usable weight and non-negative freight
findings.interpretation: Freight has a large fixed component (handling/leg cost) that dominates light items, so the marginal cost of extra weight is low. Heavy items pay more in absolute terms but less per kilogram.
findings.recommendation: Bundle light items to amortise the fixed freight component, and price or promote heavy items with freight-aware thresholds so the per-kg economics are visible.
findings.limitations: Freight is the customer charge, not carrier cost. Weight comes from the product catalogue and a few products have missing/invalid weight (kept in an 'unknown' bucket).
findings.correlation_note: The weight/freight correlation is mechanical and expected, not a behavioural causal link; size and distance are additional unmodelled drivers.
findings.headline: Freight is 16.57% of merchandise sales; freight per kg falls from R$ 112.70 to R$ 4.03 from the lightest to the heaviest bucket.

findings.title: Known data-quality gaps and how they affect the KPIs
findings.business_question: Which data defects could change a business conclusion if ignored?
findings.method: Count the rows affected by each documented defect directly in the database and map each to the KPIs it touches.
findings.result: orders with no line items: 775; orders with no payment record: 1; orders with no review: 768; orders with no delivery date (excluded from delivery KPIs): 2,965; payment rows with a non-positive value: 9; products with no category: 0; category names with no English mapping: 3; orders whose duplicate reviews were collapsed to one: 547; customer_unique_ids spanning two states: 39; customer ZIPs with no usable geolocation centroid: 158 (167 geolocation rows in total).
findings.period_population: 99,441 orders, 98,673 reviews, and associated dimension rows
findings.interpretation: None of these defects invalidate the headline KPIs - each is either immaterial in size or explicitly excluded and documented - but the delivery KPIs carry the largest population gap (orders with no delivery date), and any distance-based geography work is limited because some customer ZIPs have no usable centroid.
findings.recommendation: Carry these counts as a data-health panel in the dashboard, and define the eligible population on every KPI card. Treat the no-delivery-date gap as the first target for upstream data capture.
findings.limitations: These are defects detectable within the export; systematic issues in the source process (e.g. events never logged) cannot be counted here.
findings.correlation_note: Data-quality counts are descriptive and do not claim causal impact.
findings.headline: The largest gap is delivery dates: 2,965 orders lack one and sit outside every delivery KPI; 775 orders carry no line items.
